idiom_name: component-local useState<T> / useReducer in the smallest component; lifted state typed once in its owner as value + updater props
implementation_notes: The mechanism is React's: a hook call in the component that reads the value declares the cell (useState<T> for a single value, useReducer for a discriminated state machine), and only the owning component and its children re-render, so colocation keeps the update scope minimal. TypeScript adds the boundary documentation: state that stays local is declared with its own type inside the component and never appears in props, while anything lifted is typed once in the owner and passed down as a value plus an updater function, so the ownership boundary is explicit in the signature. The replacement for the classic structure (one typed store slice for everything) is therefore local typed cells plus deliberate lifting; the store form remains justified for genuinely global, cross-route state, and a union type is the usual way to keep a colocated multi-case cell honest.
pitfalls: useState infers its type from the initial value, so unions and nullable cells need an explicit type argument (useState<Status>('idle')) or the type widens and later assignments fail.

When state is lifted, its type must live with the owner: a child that re-declares its own copy of the type creates two definitions that drift, and missing the updater in the props makes the child silently read-only.

A context created with an undefined default makes the consumer's value possibly-undefined; colocated state avoids that class of error, so do not reach for context when the value is only used in one subtree.
